meta.description: No — C.S. Lewis never wrote this. It appears in none of his works; the earliest documented version is James R. Sherman's 1982 book “Rejection.”

answer.label: Not C.S. Lewis — traced to James R. Sherman
answer.authorDates: American self-help author · earliest documented source (1982)
answer.sourceLine: This exact wording appears in none of C.S. Lewis’s works, and the C.S. Lewis Foundation says it “doesn’t sound like him.” Quote Investigator ↗ traces the earliest documented form to James R. Sherman’s 1982 book Rejection — “You can’t go back and make a new start, but you can start right now and make a brand new ending.” The popular Lewis wording is a later paraphrase with no primary source.

source.excerpt: You can’t go back and make a new start, but you can start right now and make a brand new ending.
trail: Quote Investigator credits James R. Sherman’s 1982 book Rejection ↗ as the earliest documented instance and calls the C.S. Lewis attribution unsupported.
The C.S. Lewis Foundation’s Steve Elmore told Check Your Fact ↗ he was “fairly sure” Lewis did not write it, as “it doesn’t quite sound like him.”
William O’Flaherty, author of The Misquotable C.S. Lewis, confirmed on Essential C.S. Lewis ↗ that the words appear nowhere in Lewis’s published work.
Zig Ziglar used a version of the saying but credited it to a “Carl Bard,” per Quote Investigator ↗ — another sign the line has no settled author.
source.excerptNote: The earliest documented wording, from James R. Sherman’s 1982 book Rejection. The C.S. Lewis version circulating online is a smoothed-over paraphrase attached to a famous name.

source.rightsNote: The exact wording credited to C.S. Lewis is an unsourced internet paraphrase, so no rights status can be asserted for it. The closest documented origin — James R. Sherman’s 1982 book Rejection — uses different words and would itself be in-copyright.

author.name: James R. Sherman
author.heading: Who actually wrote it
author.metaLine: American self-help author · earliest documented source of the saying (1982)
author.bio: James R. Sherman, Ph.D. was an American self-help writer who ran Pathway Books in Golden Valley, Minnesota, and published a series of short motivational titles in the early 1980s. His 1982 book Rejection contains the earliest documented form of this saying — “You can’t go back and make a new start, but you can start right now and make a brand new ending” — which later mutated into the smoother wording now pinned, wrongly, on C.S. Lewis.

misattribution.heading: How it got pinned on C.S. Lewis
misattribution.intro: This is a textbook feel-good misattribution: a punchy line of self-help wisdom migrated onto one of the internet’s favorite quotation magnets. Lewis never wrote it.

items.why: The line is absent from all of Lewis’s published writing. The C.S. Lewis Foundation’s Steve Elmore said it “doesn’t quite sound like him,” and specialist William O’Flaherty lists it among Lewis misquotes, per Check Your Fact ↗.

A variant — “Nobody can go back and start a new beginning, but anyone can start today and make a new ending” — is often credited to a “Maria Robinson,” but Quote Investigator ↗ finds no solid source for her either.
Zig Ziglar used a form of the saying but credited an otherwise-undocumented “Carl Bard,” per Quote Investigator ↗ — not claiming it as his own.

misattribution.truthLine: The earliest documented version is James R. Sherman’s in his 1982 book Rejection; every attribution to C.S. Lewis is unsupported, per Quote Investigator ↗.

context.heading: Why the mix-up sticks
lead: The sentiment — you can’t rewrite your past, but you can still change how your story ends — is warm, quotable, and vaguely spiritual, which is exactly the profile of lines that drift toward famous Christian writers like C.S. Lewis. Once a name that respectable is attached, the quote spreads faster and is questioned less.

Ironically, Lewis did write something adjacent in Mere Christianity — about how turning back when you’re on the wrong road is the most progressive move — which may be why the misattribution feels plausible. But feeling Lewis-like is not the same as being written by Lewis.
context.pull: You can’t rewrite the past — but you can rewrite whose name is on the quote.
